title: Graphs, degrees, and trees
summary: A simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges. The sum of the degrees is twice the number of edges, and a tree is a connected acyclic graph, equivalently a connected graph with one fewer edge than vertices.
intuition:
An undirected simple graph is a finite set of vertices and a set of edges, each edge a pair of distinct vertices, with at most one edge per pair. A directed graph uses ordered pairs instead, so the edge from $u$ to $v$ is not the edge from $v$ to $u$. A loop, an edge from a vertex to itself, and a second edge on a pair that already has one, both take the graph outside the simple case. A weighted edge is the same pair with a number attached. The number is the cost or the length that a later shortest-path algorithm will add up; the representation just has to store it.

The handshaking lemma is the first numerical check. In an undirected graph each edge contributes to two degrees, so $\sum_v \deg(v)=2|E|$. The sum is even, and therefore the number of odd-degree vertices is even. An even sum is necessary and not sufficient: a sequence can pass the parity test and still be impossible to draw. In a directed graph the matching identity is different. Each edge leaves one vertex and enters one vertex, so the sum of the out-degrees equals $|E|$, and the sum of the in-degrees equals $|E|$ as well.

A path is a walk that does not repeat a vertex. A cycle in a simple undirected graph is a closed path of length at least $3$. A graph is connected when every pair of vertices is joined by a path. For a finite undirected graph the following are equivalent: the graph is a tree, meaning connected and acyclic; the graph is connected and $|E|=|V|-1$. A connected graph with a cycle has at least $|V|$ edges. Two representations matter for the algorithms that follow. An adjacency matrix uses $\Theta(|V|^2)$ cells and answers "is there an edge?" in constant time. An adjacency list uses $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ space and lists the neighbours of a vertex in time proportional to its degree.

definitions.body: Undirected, no loops, and no two edges on the same pair of vertices. The maximum number of edges on $n$ vertices is $n(n-1)/2$.
In an undirected graph, the number of edges incident to a vertex. In a directed graph, the out-degree is the number of edges leaving the vertex and the in-degree is the number entering it.
A path does not repeat a vertex. A cycle is a closed path; in a simple undirected graph its length is at least $3$. The graph is connected when a path joins every pair of vertices.
A finite undirected graph that is connected and acyclic. Equivalently, it is connected and $|E|=|V|-1$. Adding any missing edge creates exactly one cycle.
An edge stored with a number. An adjacency matrix stores that number in the corresponding cell, using a sentinel for a missing edge. An adjacency list stores the neighbour together with the weight.

formulas.name: Handshaking
formulas.note: Undirected graphs. The directed form is $\sum_v \mathrm{out}(v)=\sum_v \mathrm{in}(v)=|E|$.

formulas.name: Tree edge count
formulas.note: Together with connectedness, this is equivalent to being connected and acyclic.

formulas.name: Space of the two representations
formulas.note: Adjacency lists versus an adjacency matrix. A weighted list stores a weight beside each neighbour.

properties: The number of odd-degree vertices in an undirected graph is even, because the degree sum is $2|E|$.
A finite undirected graph is a tree if and only if it is connected and acyclic, if and only if it is connected and $|E|=|V|-1$.
A connected undirected graph with $|E|\ge |V|$ contains a cycle. A tree on $n\ge 2$ vertices has a vertex of degree $1$.
An adjacency list is the representation on which BFS and DFS run in $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ time. A matrix forces a $\Theta(|V|^2)$ scan to find every neighbour.
Between any two vertices of a tree there is exactly one path. The same graph with one extra edge has exactly one cycle.

examples.title: A path on six vertices is a tree
examples.prompt: Vertices $A,B,C,D,E,F$ and edges $AB, BC, CD, DE, EF$. Check the degree sum, the edge count, and whether the graph is a tree.
steps: The degrees are $1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1$. Their sum is $10$, so $|E|=10/2=5$. There are two odd-degree vertices, and $2$ is even.
The drawing is a single path, so it is connected, and a path does not repeat a vertex, so it has no cycle.
Also $|V|-1=5=|E|$. Connectedness together with this edge count is the tree test, and it agrees with connectedness together with the absence of a cycle.
examples.answer: The graph is a tree: $5$ edges on $6$ vertices, connected and acyclic. The degree sum $10$ matches $2|E|$.

examples.title: Parity is not enough, and the matrix is quadratic
examples.prompt: The sequence $3, 3, 3, 1$ has even sum. Does a simple undirected graph realise it? Separately, how large are the two representations of a graph with $100$ vertices and $200$ edges?
steps: The sum is $3+3+3+1=10$, which is even, so handshaking would require $|E|=5$ if a graph existed. The parity test does not reject the sequence.

Suppose the three degree-$3$ vertices exist on four vertices. Each of them is adjacent to all three others, including the remaining vertex. That remaining vertex would then have degree at least $3$, not $1$. The sequence is not graphic.

For $|V|=100$ and $|E|=200$, the matrix has $100^2=10000$ cells. The undirected adjacency lists store $2\times 200=400$ neighbour references. The list bound is $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$; the matrix bound is $\Theta(|V|^2)$.
examples.answer: No simple graph has degrees $3, 3, 3, 1$. A $100$-vertex, $200$-edge graph uses $10000$ matrix cells and $400$ list references.

traps: Using $\sum \deg(v)=2|E|$ for the out-degrees of a directed graph. The sum of the out-degrees equals $|E|$, not $2|E|$.
Treating an even degree sum as a guarantee that the sequence is graphic. $3, 3, 3, 1$ sums to $10$ and is not the degree sequence of any simple graph.
Calling a connected graph a tree because it has $n$ vertices, without checking $|E|=n-1$ or the absence of a cycle. One extra edge creates a cycle.
Quoting $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ space for an adjacency matrix. That bound is the list. The matrix is $\Theta(|V|^2)$ even when the graph is a tree.
python:
degrees = [1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1]
assert sum(degrees) == 10 and sum(degrees) // 2 == 5 == 6 - 1
assert sum(d % 2 for d in degrees) % 2 == 0
target = [3, 3, 3, 1]
assert sum(target) % 2 == 0
from itertools import combinations
possible = list(combinations(range(4), 2))
found = False
for mask in range(1 << len(possible)):
    got = [0, 0, 0, 0]
    for bit, (u, v) in enumerate(possible):
        if mask & (1 << bit):
            got[u] += 1
            got[v] += 1
    found = found or sorted(got) == sorted(target)
assert not found
assert 100 * 100 == 10000 and 2 * 200 == 400
print(sum(degrees) // 2, 10000)

questions.stem: An undirected graph has degree sequence $2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2$. The handshaking lemma gives $|E|$ equal to
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $6$.

The degrees sum to $12$, and $|E|$ is half of that sum, so $|E|=6$. Option B is the degree sum itself, which is $2|E|$, not $|E|$. This sequence is a disjoint union of cycles, or one $6$-cycle, and both have $6$ edges.

questions.stem: A finite undirected graph is connected and has $15$ vertices and $14$ edges. The graph is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, a tree.

A finite undirected graph is a tree exactly when it is connected and $|E|=|V|-1$. Here $14=15-1$, and the graph is connected, so it is acyclic as well. Option C has the equivalence backwards: this pair of conditions rules a cycle out. It does not leave the question open.
options: forced to contain a cycle by the count $|E|=|V|-1$

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of finite undirected graphs?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

Each undirected edge contributes $1$ to two degrees, so the degree sum is $2|E|$, and an even sum forces an even number of odd degrees. An adjacency matrix stores $\Theta(|V|^2)$ cells whether or not the edges are sparse; an adjacency list stores $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$. Option C is false: a tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges, not $n$.
options: The sum of the degrees equals twice the number of edges.
The number of odd-degree vertices is even.
A tree on $n$ vertices has $n$ edges.
An adjacency matrix uses $\Theta(|V|^2)$ cells, and an adjacency list uses $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$ space.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

A simple undirected graph has at most one edge per pair, and there are $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. In a directed graph each edge contributes to exactly one out-degree, so the out-degrees sum to $|E|$. Adding an edge to a tree joins two vertices that already had one path, and the new edge plus that path is the only new cycle. Option C is false: a connected graph with a cycle has at least $|V|$ edges.
options: A simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices has at most $n(n-1)/2$ edges.
In a directed graph, the sum of the out-degrees equals the number of edges.
A connected undirected graph that contains a cycle satisfies $|E|=|V|-1$.
Adding one edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle.

questions.stem: A connected acyclic undirected graph has $18$ vertices. How many edges does it have?
questions.solution:
The answer is **17**.

A finite undirected graph that is connected and acyclic is a tree, and a tree satisfies $|E|=|V|-1$. With $18$ vertices the edge count is $17$.
